subject: Climate & Environment
title: Cape Town's Day Zero
description: Learn Cape Town's Day Zero in one minute.

hook.text: In 2018, Cape Town nearly became the first major city to run out of water completely.

buildup.text: Three years of drought emptied reservoirs to 13% capacity. Rationing began at 50 liters per person.

discovery.text: Citizens lined up at springs. Farmers lost crops. The date reservoirs would hit zero was published.

twist.text: Day Zero never arrived. Strict rationing and emergency measures cut usage by 50% in months.

climax.text: But the underlying problem — over-reliance on rain-fed dams — remains for many cities.

punchline.text: Cape Town was a warning. The next city might not be so lucky.

quiz.question: What was 'Day Zero' in Cape Town?
options: The projected date taps would run dry
The first day of rain after the drought

details.summary: In 2018, Cape Town nearly became the first major city to run out of water after three years of historic drought depleted its reservoirs. Day Zero, when taps would be turned off, was averted only through aggressive rationing, cutting per capita use from 200 to 50 liters per day.
details.whyItMatters: Cape Town's crisis was a wake-up call for cities worldwide. It demonstrated how quickly water supplies can fail and how dramatic behavioral change can be mobilized under extreme pressure.
takeaways: Cape Town nearly ran out of water after a three-year drought
Per capita use was slashed from 200 to 50 liters per day
The crisis highlighted vulnerability of single-source systems

faq.question: How did Cape Town avoid Day Zero?
faq.answer: The city imposed severe water restrictions, limiting residents to 50 liters per day. Agricultural water was curtailed, pressure was reduced, and public awareness campaigns drove behavioral change. Rains eventually returned, but the city was within weeks of shutting off taps.

faq.question: Could Day Zero happen to other cities?
faq.answer: Yes. Sao Paulo, Chennai, Mexico City, and many other major cities have faced severe water crises. Climate change, population growth, and aging infrastructure make Day Zero scenarios increasingly plausible for cities relying on limited or single water sources.
